Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Ukrainian plasma-derived drugs producer Biofarma has doubled its planned investment in a pharmaceutical plant in Oradea, western Romania, with the first stage of the project now valued at EUR 85 million, Bihoreanul reported, cited by Economedia.ro . The investment is EUR 48 million above the minimum amount announced in 2024, when the construction of the pharmaceutical factory was presented as the largest investment of that year in the industrial parks managed by the Oradea Local Development Agency. The Oradea project is planned in four stages, according to Biofarma representatives cited by Interfax-Ukraine. The company has not disclosed the total value of the investment, providing only the cost of bringing the first stage into operation. "We have already completed the construction of the building, and by September 1 we will finish connecting the entire engineering infrastructure. We have already ordered the filling line," Biofarma Plasma President Kostiantyn Yefymenko told Ukrainian media. The first stage will involve putting the production line into operation. The facility is planned to have the capacity to process up to 1.2 million litres of frozen human plasma a year. Biofarma was founded in 1965 and initially focused on developing technologies for the production of plasma-derived medicines. The company describes itself as operating one of the largest plasma fractionation facilities in Eastern Europe. The Oradea plant forms part of Biofarma’s expansion outside Ukraine, with the investment adding pharmaceutical production capacity in Romania. iulian@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Alena Butor/Dreamstime.com ) Normal Healthcare Ukraine’s Biofarma reportedly doubles investment in Romanian plants at EUR 85 mln 30 July 2026 Iulian Ernst Like this article? Photograph: Luke Massey Country diary Birds Country diary: A pocket rocket of rewilding – and a success in the face of opposition Asturias, Spain : I visit a farm that is thrilling in its ecological abundance, created in just eight years Amy-Jane Beer Wed 26 Aug 2026 00.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O n a rocky 13-hectare pocket in the foothills of the Picos de Europa, Luke Massey and Katie Stacey are raising children, dogs, cattle, chicken, ducks, geese and eyebrows. In their eight years here, the farm they call Wild Finca has become a mass of scrub, with scattered large trees and dozens of clearings that Luke calls fields, but which look more like tiny irregular glades, riddled with trails and hemmed all around by the blackthorn, gorse and bramble that has sprung up around the tumbled remains of drystone walls. If Wild Finca is a forever home to the Massey-Staceys, it is a whole world to nature. Witness the butterflies and wasp spiders, the snakes, lizards, hedgehogs and sparrows, and the thousand-piece cricket orchestra that performs each evening as the glow-worms light up. It offers denning and roosting sites for foxes, pine martens, badgers and 17 species of bat, feeding opportunities for roe deer and wild boar, several species of eagle and vulture, and a pit stop for others such as the nightingale I heard singing in early morning mist. View image in fullscreen The Wild Finca farm in Asturias, northern Spain. Photograph: Luke Massey It is a multifaceted ecological hub, which Luke and Katie say disproves the idea that rewilding can only happen at scale. Wildlife does not see boundaries, and good land is good land. From a UK perspective, all of Asturias is thrillingly wild, and our time here is a tonic. But it is no ecological utopia. Development for tourism appears underregulated, if the vast techno festival we see setting up nearby and the insane duck-race-cum-traffic-jam of 3,000 plastic rental kayaks bumping daily down the River Salla are anything to go by. Corruption, commercialism, hunting and small-minded conservatism have challenged Luke and Katie at every turn, but they have allies too: kindly neighbours; the vet who regards their tiny herd as the healthiest cattle in the area; the retired police chief who repeatedly backs them; and the octogenarian who tips them off about an animal whose name is best spoken in a whisper – el lobo , the wolf. The land here is well in range of packs living in the Picos, but the Asturian government has just announced a new cull of 67 out of 400 animals. The sanctuary of Wild Finca will not help them until wider attitudes change. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian Homelessness Burnham to double spending on homelessness amid drive to end rough sleeping by Christmas Downing Street will allocate a further £432m in this week’s budget, bringing total funding for finding a ‘lasting solution’ to nearly £900m Rowena Mason Whitehall editor Sun 25 Oct 2026 18.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham is to double spending on ending rough sleeping to almost £900m by the end of the current parliament, as he steps up efforts to get people off the streets by Christmas. The prime minister has pledged to offer every rough sleeper in England a safe route off the streets or wider support as a central part of his premiership. As he prepared for a Downing Street summit on ending rough sleeping on Monday, Burnham said the budget would bring a further £432m commitment to helping to tackle homelessness. The sum is on top of an initial £442m from Ministry of Housing , Communities and Local Government budgets that will be allocated to the problem before March 2027. Speaking ahead of the meeting, which will bring together charities and businesses, Burnham said: “Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life. It’s a thing governments either choose to accept or don’t. “Well, I don’t accept it. That’s why we’re doubling funding so that people aren’t just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this parliament too. “But we can’t do it alone. If we’re going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this. So today we’re bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts.” Andy Burnham calls on wider society to help end rough sleeping by Christmas Read more Burnham’s mission to end rough sleeping is already under way with just two months to go before his deadline. There are specialist outreach teams and new accommodation spaces operating in Coventry, and further provision is being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden over the coming weeks. The additional funding is being provided in an attempt to solve the problem of rough sleeping in the longer term. As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced schemes such as A Bed Every Night to offer emergency accommodation, but while the number of rough sleepers fell, it then began to increase again. Burnham has previously said this was because “we were the only place providing that level of support and, understandably, people then travelled to Greater Manchester to access that support”. He has said ending rough sleeping across the country will only be possible “if all areas are pulling in the same direction, and that’s what this funding is designed to achieve”. 11:13 Will Andy Burnham get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas? – The Latest The prime minister’s rough sleeping summit on Monday will bring together businesses, charities, housing providers and local leaders as they attempt to create more lasting changes. Alongside the government, other organisations are making pledges towards solving the problem, with the National Housing Federation working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use. Virgin Media O2 will provide practical digital support to frontline organisations, while the charities St Mungo’s and Haircuts4Homeless will work with L’Oréal on hair salons and wellbeing provision for those who have been sleeping rough. View image in fullscreen Rayner, pictured with Burnham at a homeless accommodation centre in Newcastle this year, said ending rough sleeping was a ‘big ambition’. Photograph: Lauren Hurley/No 10 Downing Street Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said it was a “big ambition” and the government would “not back down from making sure everyone has the offer of a route off the streets this Christmas”. She said: “The first step is giving people a roof over their head and freedom from the nightly struggle to find somewhere safe to sleep. But Christmas is only the beginning and that’s why we will keep working together to tackle the root causes of homelessness and end rough sleeping for good.” The homelessness charity Shelter welcomed the announcement. Its acting CEO, Mairi MacRae, said the funding showed “the government understands that a safe home is not a privilege, it is a necessity”. However, the Conservatives dismissed the move, with Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, accusing the government of wanting to spend too much money on ending rough sleeping. Why are rough sleepers dying a stone’s throw from luxury waterfront houses in Victoria? Read more “Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester,” she said. “Under Labour , rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers’ money and more empty promises.” Referring to the chancellor, Lam said: “[John] Healey must use his budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices. Instead of piling more costs on to hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers’ money.” Explore more on these topics Homelessness Andy Burnham Angela Rayner Labour Budget 2026 Housing Poverty news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland
